extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Catholic dogmatic theology (seminarians, theologians)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes doctrinal criteria about sanctifying grace, justification, merit, and related canons and Scriptural/theological authorities as presented in a dogmatic treatise on grace and merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of brethren as sign of passing from death to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Quia transivimus de morte ad vitam. Unde scimus? Quia diligimus fratres. (If in one’s heart one finds brotherly charity, one may be sure one has passed from death to life.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a criterion of spiritual life and justification: self-examination for fraternal charity is evidence of having passed from death to life (cf. I John commentary, Tract. in Ioa.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of sanctifying grace according to measure and cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Iustitiam in nobis recipientes, unusquisque suam secundum mensuram, quam Spiritus Sanctus partitur singulis prout vult, et secundum propriam cuiusque dispositionem et cooperationem. (Grace is received in each according to the measure given by the Holy Spirit and according to each person's disposition and cooperation.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine that sanctifying grace varies in degree among the faithful; allocation is by the Holy Spirit but also depends on personal disposition and cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justified persons grow in justice by cooperating faith with good works
rubrics_metrics.description: Iustificati ... in ipsa iustitia per Christi gratiam accepta, cooperante fide bonis operibus crescunt atque magis iustificantur. (Those justified by Christ’s grace grow in justice by faith cooperating with good works.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms that justification, once received, does not remain static but can increase through cooperative good works; appeals to Tridentine formulations and patristic/supporting theological authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial that accepted justice cannot be preserved or augmented by good works is condemned
rubrics_metrics.description: Si quis dixerit, iustitiam acceptam non conservari atque etiam augeri coram Deo per bona opera ... anathema sit. (It is anathematized to say that accepted justice cannot be preserved and increased before God by good works.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Trent canons condemning opinions that reduce good works to mere signs rather than causes of increase in grace; used as a normative corrective against contrary views.

rubrics_metrics.name: A justified person can lose grace and justification through mortal sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Si quis hominem semel iustificatum dixerit amplius peccare non posse neque gratiam amittere ... anathema sit. (It is anathematized to claim that one once justified cannot sin any more or lose grace.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tridentine canons assert the real possibility of falling from grace by mortal sin; used to reject absolutist claims denying loss of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: No one in this life is without sin; degree of sin varies
rubrics_metrics.description: Induti sunt sancti iustitiâ ..., alius magis, alius minus; et nemo hic vivit sine peccato et hoc alius magis, alius minus: optimus autem est qui minimum. (The saints partake of justice more or less; no one here lives without sin; degrees vary.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthology of theological and patristic statements emphasizing human imperfection in this life; used as background for discussing gradual growth and fragility of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good works performed in the state of grace are meritorious and deserve reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Debetur merces bonis operibus, si fiant; sed gratia, quae non debetur, praecedit ut fiant. (A reward is due for good works if they are done; yet grace, which is not owed, precedes so that they may be done.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tridentine and doctrinal material affirm that good works done in grace merit reward (including eternal reward), while maintaining priority of gratuitous grace; includes multiple conciliar canons and patristic citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good works of adopted children merit insofar as they conform to divine law, not merely because they are performed by the Spirit of adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Opera bona a filiis adoptionis facta non accipiunt rationem meriti ... sed tantum ex eo, quod sunt conformia legi quodque per ea praestatur obedientia legi. (Good works by adopted children do not obtain the status of merit merely because they are done by the Spirit of adoption, but because they conform to the law and effect obedience.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies the basis of merit: conformity to divine law and obedience grounds merit, rather than merely the presence of the Spirit in the actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit of eternal life primarily pertains to charity; other virtues are subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Meritum vitae aeternae primo pertinet ad caritatem, ad alias autem virtutes secundario, secundum quod earum actus a caritate imperantur. (Merit of eternal life primarily belongs to charity; other virtues secondarily insofar as their acts are ordered by charity.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Aquinas (Summae) and later commentators: charity (caritas) is the fundamental motive/condition for acts to be meritorious toward eternal life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific intention is required for merit; general reference to God is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Non sufficere, si quis ad initium anni vel mensis vel etiam diei generali quadam intentione referat omnia sua futura opera in Deum, sed necesse esse ut illud ipsum opus particulare referatur in Deum, quod postea faciendum est. (It is not sufficient to refer all future works to God by a general intention; the particular act itself must be referred to God.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From De Iustificatione: for works to be meritorious the particular act must be explicitly referred to God at the time it is done; mere broad or general intentions do not secure merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification is gratuitous; antecedent acts (faith/works) do not make grace owed
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratis autem iustificari ideo dicimur, quia nihil eorum quae iustificationem praecedunt, sive fides, sive opera, ipsam iustificationis gratiam promeretur; si enim gratia est, iam non ex operibus, alioquin ... gratia iam non est gratia. (We are said to be justified freely because nothing which precedes justification — whether faith or works — merits that grace.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tridentine teaching reiterated: while works and faith have a role, initial justification remains a gratuitous gift of God and is not owed to preceding human acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between merit 'condign' and 'congruum' (condign vs congruous merit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplex est meritum. Unum quod innititur iustitiae et istud est meritum condigni; aliud quod soli misericordiae innititur, quod dicitur meritum congrui. (There are two kinds of merit: one founded on justice — meritum condigni; another founded on mercy — meritum congrui.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains the classical distinction: condign merit implies a justice-like claim (strictly speaking under divine ordination), whereas congruous merit depends on God’s mercy; theological treatments and authorities (Aquinas, commentators) are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good works after justification can increase grace and merit (augmentation of grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoc vero iustitiae incrementum petit sancta Ecclesia, quum orat: Da nobis, Domine, fidei, spei et caritatis augmentum. (The Holy Church prays for an increase of justice; good works cooperate to augment sanctifying grace.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites Scripture, Council of Trent, and theologians to affirm that sanctifying grace can be increased through right acts and dispositions; canonical condemnations reject opinions denying such augmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer (impetration) obtains graces for others but is distinct from merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Impetratio orationis innititur misericordiae, meritum autem condigni innititur iustitiae. Et ideo multa orando impetrat homo ex divina misericordia, quae tamen non meretur secundum iustitiam. (The obtaining by prayer rests on mercy; condign merit rests on justice. Many things are obtained by prayer from divine mercy, which are not merited in justice.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between what may be obtained by intercession (impetration) and what is merited strictly in justice; includes examples (Patriarchs, saints, intercession for the living) and theological references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal goods can be meritorious insofar as they are ordered to help virtuous acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Si temporalia bona considerentur, prout sunt utilia ad opera virtutum, quibus perducimur in vitam aeternam, secundum hoc directe et simpliciter cadunt sub merito. (Temporal goods, insofar as they serve the operations of the virtues that lead to eternal life, directly fall under merit.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that temporal goods are meritorious only in relation to their use in promoting virtuous acts directed toward eternal ends; otherwise they are not simply meritorious in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: God’s promise of reward does not make God a debtor; merit presupposes divine ordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Non sequitur quod Deus efficiatur simpliciter debitor nobis, sed sibi ipsi, inquantum debitum est, ut sua ordinatio impleatur. (It does not follow that God becomes simply debtor to us; rather He binds Himself by His own ordinance to fulfil promises.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological nuance distinguishing human merit from creating a literal debt in God: God’s promise grounds the certainty of reward without making God intrinsically a debtor; cited from Aquinas and commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards and punishments correspond to works (scriptural principle of retribution according to works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qui reddet unicuique secundum opera eius ... Unusquisque autem propriam mercedem accipiet secundum suum laborem. (Scriptural and theological assertion that God will render to each according to his works; each will receive recompense according to his labor.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scripture and theological sources are cited repeatedly to support the proportionality of reward/punishment to moral conduct; used to justify teaching on merit and final recompense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of erroneous propositions denying necessity of charity or meritoriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. Baii ... sensu est probabilis ... Prop. damnata: 'Probabile est, ne singulis quidem rigorose quinquenniis per se obligare praeceptum caritatis erga Deum.' and other condemned propositions (Baius, Quietism, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise references specific condemned propositions (e.g., Baius, certain Jansenist or Quietist claims) to indicate doctrinal boundaries: positions denying the necessity of charity, denying meritoriousness of good works, or minimizing human cooperation are explicitly rejected.
